title: GC Pulse 2025: In-House Legal Tech Adoption Surging as Gen AI Gains Ground

kp.k: In-house legal technology use rises, driven by generative AI
kp.d: Legal Business reports findings from GC Pulse 2025, conducted in association with Thomson Reuters and drawing on over 150 general counsel and senior lawyers. The share of corporate legal departments using legal technology frequently or all the time rose from 34% in 2024 to 44% in 2025. The article attributes much of this growth to generative AI entering daily workflows; the usage percentages concern legal technology generally, not AI alone.
qs: GC Pulse 2025, which was conducted by Legal Business in association with Thomson Reuters, has revealed that 44% of corporate legal departments are now using legal technology frequently or all the time — a sharp rise from 34% in 2024.
The survey found much of this growth in usage is being driven by generative AI, with legal teams integrating it into their daily workflows faster than ever before.

kp.k: Corporate support grows for legal technology investment
kp.d: The article reports growing corporate support for legal technology investment amid tight budgets and increasing leadership, matter-management and compliance demands on GCs. Nearly one-third (32%) found technology purchase approval easy or very easy. Eighty percent expected to devote as much as 20% of legal budgets to technology in 2025, compared with 68% in 2024, with AI expected to drive much of the increase. These are reported expectations rather than completed expenditure.
qs: Nearly one-third (32%) of the GCs surveyed said they now found it easy or very easy to secure approval for technology purchases.
Eighty percent of respondents expect to devote as much as 20% of their legal budgets to technology this year, up from 68% in 2024, with AI expected to drive much of this increase.

kp.k: Alliance Pharma reports dramatic NDA automation time savings
kp.d: Max Freeman-Inglis, Alliance Pharma's head of legal operations, describes executive enthusiasm for AI and a progression from organising contract data to a fully automated NDA system. He reports turnaround falling from two to three weeks to two to three hours, offering a measurable result for the board. This is a practitioner account of an implementation, not a survey-wide finding or a separately quantified generative AI effect.
qs: Our C-suite are huge on AI – they love it, see the benefits, and there’s a real push to use it. We started with the pure data piece: uploading contracts and getting the data sorted. Now, we’ve got a fully automated system for non-disclosure agreements (NDAs). What used to take two to three weeks now takes two to three hours. That’s an easy metric to show the board.

kp.k: Reported trust in AI rises substantially
kp.d: The survey reports 40% of respondents expressing trust in AI as a legal resource, up from 21% in 2024. The article also reports that only 3% of legal professionals considered AI not yet dependable, down from 11% in 2024. These findings describe perceptions of reliability rather than measured accuracy or verification outcomes.
qs: The survey also found that perception of AI as a reliable legal resource has nearly doubled within the GC community, with 40% of respondents now expressing trust in the technology, compared to 21% last year.
Only 3% of legal professionals maintain that AI is not yet dependable; down sharply from 11% in 2024.

kp.k: Spending intentions outpace full generative AI integration
kp.d: Despite increased trust, the article characterises implementation as measured: 86% of GCs plan to maintain or increase AI-related spending, but only 11% have fully integrated generative AI tools into operations. Respondents identify automation, due diligence and contract lifecycle management as major opportunities for AI, rather than reporting universal deployment in those activities.
qs: Although the survey found that 86% of GCs plan to maintain or increase AI-related spending, only 11% have fully integrated generative AI tools into their operations.
When asked where they saw the biggest use case opportunities for AI to enhance their work, GCs pinpointed automation, due diligence and contract lifecycle management (CLM) as areas for growth.

kp.k: Workflow automation remains valuable alongside generative AI
kp.d: Thomson Reuters associate general counsel Alex Graydon argues that established automation remains valuable despite generative AI's prominence. He describes document automation supporting self-service NDAs since around 2015 and a HighQ-based legal intake system collecting information, allocating lawyers, managing workflows and reporting data. His recommendation is to retain workflow and document automation while layering AI onto it for additional insights and value.
qs: We’ve had a document automation product since around 2015, which allowed us to automate and release self-serve NDAs to the business, and we’ve expanded that automation model.

We use it for work intake: asking a series of questions, collecting answers, allocating lawyers, managing workflows, and reporting data. But we can now layer on AI to this to extract insights and value.

For those just starting their tech transformation journey, it’s worth remembering automation and combining these tools with Gen AI can be powerful, but automation of workflows and document creation remains extremely valuable for many businesses.

kp.k: Agentic AI and routine lawyer adoption are anticipated
kp.d: The article presents agentic AI capable of complex, multi-step legal processes as a future frontier, not an established deployment finding. Separately, Colt Technology Services deputy GC Alessandro Galtieri predicts that within five years AI use will become as normal for lawyers as email is today.
qs: Looking ahead, the survey points to agentic AI – autonomous systems capable of handling complex, multi-step legal processes – as the next frontier.
Five years from now, a lawyer who doesn’t use AI will be like a lawyer today who doesn’t use email.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Stanley reports that generative AI is driving increased in-house legal technology adoption, support for technology investment and confidence in AI, while full operational integration remains limited.
pts.d: Reporting GC Pulse 2025, Stanley states that frequent or constant legal technology use increased from 34% in 2024 to 44% in 2025 and attributes much of the growth to generative AI. She also reports that heightened AI awareness is increasing corporate support for legal technology investment: 32% find purchase approval easy or very easy, and 80% expect to allocate as much as 20% of legal budgets to technology, compared with 68% in 2024. AI is expected to drive much of the budget increase. Reported trust in AI rose from 21% to 40%, while the proportion saying AI is not yet dependable fell from 11% to 3%. These are perceptions, not measured reliability findings. Although 86% plan to maintain or increase AI spending, only 11% report fully integrating generative AI. Respondents identify automation, due diligence and contract lifecycle management as leading opportunities.

pts.k: Freeman-Inglis reports sharply faster NDA processing through automation; Graydon argues that AI can add insight to established automation rather than replace its value.
pts.d: Max Freeman-Inglis, head of legal operations at Alliance Pharma, describes an AI-supportive C-suite and a progression from organising contract data to a fully automated NDA system, reducing turnaround from two to three weeks to two to three hours. The passage does not establish that generative AI specifically caused this reduction. Alex Graydon, associate general counsel at Thomson Reuters, describes longstanding document automation and a HighQ legal intake system that collects information, allocates lawyers, manages workflows and reports data. He says AI can be layered onto these systems to extract additional insights, while workflow and document automation remain valuable independently.

pts.k: The article presents agentic AI as a future development, while Galtieri predicts that AI use will become as routine for lawyers as email.
pts.d: Stanley reports the survey's forward-looking framing of agentic AI as the next frontier for complex, multi-step legal processes. Alessandro Galtieri, deputy GC at Colt Technology Services, predicts that within five years, a lawyer not using AI will be comparable to a lawyer currently not using email. This is a prediction about AI becoming a professional norm, not a quantified forecast of job displacement or autonomous replacement of lawyers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of survey responses and practitioner accounts; the future-facing claims are forecasts rather than demonstrated outcomes.
pts.d: The adoption, budget, trust and integration figures come from GC Pulse 2025, conducted by Legal Business in association with Thomson Reuters, surveying more than 150 general counsel and senior lawyers. Comparisons with 2024 are reported, but the supplied article does not give sampling details or establish whether the same respondents participated in both years. Freeman-Inglis offers an organisational experience and a turnaround-time metric for NDA automation. Graydon offers experience with document automation and legal intake workflows at Thomson Reuters, without a quantified result for the incremental contribution of AI. The agentic-AI outlook is attributed to the survey without supporting deployment data in the article. Galtieri supports his five-year prediction with an email analogy, not a model or benchmark.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article distinguishes current adoption and 2025 spending intentions from an undated agentic-AI outlook and a five-year professional-normalisation forecast.
pts.d: Published on 15 August 2025, the article compares current survey responses with 2024. Technology budget allocations and AI spending plans are prospective intentions, not confirmed expenditure. Increased trust coexists with only 11% full generative-AI integration, qualifying the account of rapid uptake. Freeman-Inglis describes an already implemented NDA system but supplies no implementation date. Graydon traces document automation to around 2015 and frames AI's additional value in the context of existing workflows and organised intake data. The agentic-AI claim has no specified adoption deadline. Galtieri's five-year horizon implies approximately 2030.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected group is corporate in-house legal teams and the businesses they support; the closing prediction extends to lawyers generally.
pts.d: GCs, senior in-house lawyers and legal operations staff are portrayed as adopting technology under pressure to manage matters, regulatory risk and compliance within tight budgets. Corporate executives and boards influence investment approval and receive performance metrics. Business users benefit from faster NDA processing, self-service documents and structured requests for legal assistance. Legal teams may gain additional insights from AI layered onto intake and workflow systems, with further opportunities identified in due diligence and CLM. Galtieri's forecast concerns lawyers broadly. The article does not make specific claims about law-firm staffing, legal-provider market share or access to justice.
